rows.evidence: Q1: Results and discussion, Figs. 3-4 - the authors report their own sensor readings (temperature, humidity, soil moisture, water level) recorded by the ESP32 prototype on 2 May 2024 during a realistic simulation of agricultural conditions.
rows.notes: The study builds and tests an in-field IoT prototype (ESP32, DHT22, soil-moisture and ultrasonic water-level sensors, SSE web dashboard). It contains no remote sensing (satellite, UAV or aerial imagery) component, so it provides no evidence on remote sensing for water conservation. Moreover, it does not measure water use or water savings at all; it only reports sensor readings and asserts improved efficiency.

rows.evidence: Q1: Results and discussion, Figs. 3-7 - own sensor data from the prototype (e.g., temperature 22.1-28 C, humidity 39-49.1%, soil moisture 62.5-65%, water level 60-62% on 2 May 2024) and terminal/web dashboard outputs.
rows.notes: The technology (IoT sensor-based irrigation control with a web/mobile interface and threshold-triggered pumps) matches app-based smart scheduling, but the study reports no result on water conservation: no water volumes, no comparison with manual or conventional irrigation, no yield data. What it shows is that the prototype can read sensors every 20 s and push readings to a web page via Server-Sent Events, and that pumps are triggered at a 38% soil-moisture threshold and a 10% tank-level threshold. Water savings and yield stability are asserted in the abstract, discussion and conclusion without any supporting measurement. The demonstrated monitoring capability is at most a precondition for the claimed water-saving effect. The paper does state limitations (connectivity, sensor reliability, prototype scale, farmer adoption), but these cannot count because there is no own result on the claim.

rows.evidence: Q1: Results and discussion, Figs. 3-4 - own prototype readings on 2 May 2024: temperature 28 C at midday falling to 22.1 C at 5 pm, humidity 39% rising to 49.1%, soil moisture 62.5-65%, water level 60-62%.
rows.notes: The sensor ranges quoted in the review passage are indeed the study's own readings, so the monitoring part of the passage is supported. However, the passage's claim that these readings validate 'digital water control and consumption reduction under real operational conditions' goes beyond the study: no water consumption was measured, no reduction was quantified, and no comparison against a baseline was made. The authors themselves describe the test as a 'realistic simulation of agricultural conditions' with a prototype, and note that results may not apply to larger farms. Real-time monitoring is a precondition for water-saving control, not evidence of the effect.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a system-design/prototype paper: a one-day demonstration of sensor acquisition and web display, with threshold-based pump logic described but no quantified irrigation outcomes (water applied, water saved, yield). Claims of improved irrigation efficiency, reduced water use and stable yields appear only as assertions in the abstract, discussion and conclusion.
